children: In a year of surging energy costs, there is one bill that might be cheaper for tens of millions of Americans: winter heat.
Roughly 46% of American homes are warmed with natural gas, prices for which are starting the heating season about 19% lower than a year ago.

Gas prices typically rise from autumn lows as temperatures drop and furnaces are fired up. Yet energy producers, traders and federal officials have been dialing down their forecasts due to record U.S. production, ample stockpiles and expectations for a mild winter in much of the country.
Goldman Sachs analysts are among the more bearish, predicting gas prices will average $2.95 per million British thermal units this winter. November futures settled Wednesday at $2.79.

Americans who use natural gas for space heating could pay about 9% less than a year ago, or about $640 on average for the combined bills covering November through March, the Energy Information Administration estimates. Together with the mostly rural Americans who use propane, more than half of U.S. households are heated with fuels that are expected to cost less than last winter, the EIA said.

Natural gas and propane, which are often produced from the same wells, are offering respite from otherwise sky-high energy prices that soared after the war between the U.S. and Iran choked off Persian Gulf oil supplies.

Average retail gasoline prices in the U.S. are up about 40% from a year ago at roughly $4.26 a gallon, busting household budgets and driving inflation higher. Diesel has hit records and is nearly 75% more expensive than a year ago, spilling into the cost of everything from groceries and shipping to heating oil for the more than four million households warmed with it. The EIA estimates that those homes, mainly in Alaska and the Northeast, will pay an average of 21% more this winter.
Meanwhile, a climb in electricity prices has outpaced inflation and become a hot political issue as worries about the data-center build-out mount.

The EIA's forecast calls for national heating demand to be roughly the same as last year as measured in heating-degree days, a population-weighted measure of temperatures below 65 degrees Fahrenheit. That outlook varies by region, of course. Although the EIA has forecast 12% fewer heating-degree days in the Northeast, it expects 25% more in the West, and higher bills there as a result.

With weather expected to generate roughly the same national demand for heat, the big factor influencing bills is expected to be the price of gas. The fuel is piped into homes for furnaces and boilers and also burned at power plants to generate electricity.

This summer, a 24% year-over-year surge in solar-power generation helped the U.S. weather the hottest July on record without drawing down natural-gas stockpiles too far. Natural-gas inventories remained slightly above the five-year average earlier this month, according to EIA data.

Although exports of liquefied natural gas, or LNG, have hit records, so too has domestic production. U.S. gas output was up 4% in the first half of the year, and EIA expects average daily output of 122.5 billion cubic feet in 2026, a record.

The quagmire in the Strait of Hormuz is responsible for much of the additional gas. Constrained crude supply from the Middle East has lifted oil prices around the world and encouraged domestic drillers, particularly in the prolific Permian Basin in West Texas, where large volumes of gas are unearthed as a byproduct. As long as oil prices are high, Permian drillers will continue to produce gas regardless of the price, and new pipelines opened this year to carry more of it to market.

Analysts say significant gas production has also been curtailed this year and many wells have been drilled but not yet connected to pipelines, especially in Appalachia, where prices have been depressed.

Producers could unleash this supply as soon as temperatures drop and prices perk up, ultimately swamping markets and adding downward pressure to prices, energy trading firm EBW Analytics Group warned clients.
